articles/starter-care.md.title: Keeping a Sourdough Starter
articles/starter-care.md.author: Mara Ellis
articles/starter-care.md.core_argument: A starter stays active when it is fed on a fixed schedule.
key_claims: A sourdough starter needs fresh flour and water once or twice a day.
A starter kept at 100 percent hydration is easier to judge by eye.

articles/autolyse-rest.md.title: Why Bakers Rest Flour and Water
articles/autolyse-rest.md.author: Jonah Pike
articles/autolyse-rest.md.core_argument: An autolyse makes dough easier to stretch.
key_claims: An autolyse is a rest of flour and water before salt is added.
Ken Forkish uses a rest of twenty to thirty minutes.

articles/bulk-timing.md.title: Timing the Bulk Rise
articles/bulk-timing.md.author: Mara Ellis
articles/bulk-timing.md.core_argument: Bulk fermentation should be judged by the dough, not the clock.
key_claims: Bulk fermentation is the first rise of the whole dough after mixing.
A warm sourdough starter shortens bulk fermentation.

articles/levain-build.md.title: Building a Levain
articles/levain-build.md.author: Ines Varga
articles/levain-build.md.core_argument: A levain built for one bake gives a predictable rise.
key_claims: A levain is a portion of sourdough starter fed and ripened for one bake.
A ripe levain shortens bulk fermentation.

articles/high-hydration.md.title: Working with Wet Dough
articles/high-hydration.md.author: Jonah Pike
articles/high-hydration.md.core_argument: Wet doughs need a gentle mix and a long rest.
key_claims: Hydration is the weight of water divided by the weight of flour.
A long autolyse helps a high hydration dough hold its shape.

articles/home-oven.md.title: Baking Bread in a Home Oven
articles/home-oven.md.author: Ines Varga
articles/home-oven.md.core_argument: A home oven needs a pot or a stone to bake a good loaf.
key_claims: Ken Forkish bakes in a preheated cast iron pot to trap steam.
Dough at a lower hydration keeps its shape on a stone.
